verses.commentary: But to Jonah this seemed very wrong. Literally, it was evil to Jonah, a great evil. The salvation of 120,000 people angers him. Success breeds fury. The prophet opposes his own effective ministry.

I knew it! Jonah's complaint reveals his theology and his heart. He quotes Exodus 34:6, God's self-revelation to Moses. Gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in love, relenting from disaster. He knows God perfectly and hates what he knows. Orthodoxy without love.
Take my life. For the second time Jonah prefers death. In chapter 1 he chose death over obedience; here he chooses death over seeing enemies forgiven. He would rather die than share God's mercy.
Is it right for you to be angry? God's question, not condemnation. An invitation to self-examination. The prophet's emotion is itself on trial. Anger can be righteous or wicked; which is this?

Jonah went out east of the city. He builds a shelter and waits. Perhaps hoping God will change his mind and destroy them anyway. He watches Nineveh like a man watching for fire to fall. Spectator to expected judgment.

God appointed a plant. Same verb as the fish, the worm, the wind. God orchestrates comfort for his angry prophet. The plant gives shade; Jonah is very happy. His joy over a plant exceeds his joy over a city's salvation.
God appointed a worm. What God gives, God takes. The plant withers. The lesson approaches. Comfort proves temporary, a setup for teaching.

God appointed a scorching east wind. The sirocco, the desert wind that drains life. Sun blazes, prophet faints. Again: better to die than to live. Third death wish. Jonah is consistent in preferring death to God's ways.

Is it right to be angry about the plant? Same question as verse 4, now about vegetation. Yes! Angry enough to die! Jonah doubles down. He defends his rage over a bush while condemning God's mercy over a city.
You are concerned about this plant. God states the obvious. A plant Jonah did not labor over, did not grow, that appeared overnight and died overnight. It cost him nothing, yet he grieves it.

Should I not have concern for Nineveh? God's final word is a question, unanswered. 120,000 people who cannot tell right from left, moral infants. And also many animals. Even the cattle matter to God. The book ends without Jonah's response. We do not know if he learned. The question hangs over every reader: will you share God's heart for the nations, even your enemies? The book refuses closure, demanding decision.
